items.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 232 — The Lunar Dump
items.snippet: On Episode 232 of This Week In Space, Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik are joined by Chelsea Gohd to talk about the recent large data dump from the Artemis II mission.

items.title: 6 scientifically accurate star projectors to turn any room into a home planetarium
items.snippet: These six realistic star projectors are much more than mood lighting. Their projections are scientifically accurate enough to serve as actual stargazing practice, perfect for budding astronomers, young and old.

items.title: California redwoods are struggling in the heat — and it's not clear how much damage is being done
items.snippet: When temperatures rise, California redwoods slow down their rate of photosynthesis, a discovery that could have implications for the long-term survival of the iconic species.

items.title: Is the brain actually 2 nervous systems smooshed together? A new study claims it is.
items.snippet: A recent study may reshape our understanding of brain evolution and open new avenues for studying neurological diseases.

items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

items.title: Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?
items.snippet: In 1960, scientists predicted that runaway population growth would bring humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts remained surprisingly accurate for decades. But as birth rates declined and population growth slowed, the terrifying prediction unraveled, revealing how even convincing scientific models can fail when human behavior changes.

items.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
items.snippet: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. items.title: SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station
items.snippet: SpaceX just delivered some surprisingly strange cargo to the International Space Station, including tiny brain models, 3D heart tissue, and technology for making artificial retinas in space. Scientists hope these experiments could unlock new ways to treat devastating brain diseases, restore eyesight, and test future medicines. items.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
items.snippet: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.

items.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
items.snippet: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.

items.title: NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
items.snippet: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres.

items.title: James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
items.snippet: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. items.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

items.title: Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes appear to launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. The breakthrough could explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will happen.

items.title: The ambiguous costs of climate change
items.snippet: As human activity has increased temperatures globally, determining the costs directly incurred by climate change is challenging. The effects of climate change on extreme weather events—such as hurricanes and heat waves—can be locally specific and variable, and observations and climate modeling might not accurately capture those effects.

items.title: Lone, starless cloud may be a 'dark' galaxy
items.snippet: Astronomers using China's FAST radio telescope have discovered a compact cloud of hydrogen with no visible stars or galaxy around it. This could be one of the strongest candidates yet for an isolated "dark galaxy," containing nearly 500,000 times the sun's mass in neutral hydrogen. The discovery paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 24.

items.title: Red-sensitive pigments in mantis shrimp eyes act as reversible light switches
items.snippet: With about 30 visual pigments, compared to just three in humans, mantis shrimp possess a visual system that remains a mystery. Researchers from ULiège and Humboldt University in Berlin have, for the first time, analyzed these pigments one by one and discovered that some detect red light that very few animals can perceive. items.title: Electrical sliding switches graphene between magnetic states
items.snippet: In a discovery that could offer a new way to control quantum properties in two-dimensional materials, researchers at Cornell have found that electrically sliding the layers of ultrathin graphene can switch the material between distinct magnetic states that persist even after the voltage is removed.

items.title: Global survey links financial hardship to lower trust in science
items.snippet: Poor access to health care, limited local influence over research priorities and an unequal distribution of scientific benefits are undermining public confidence in science, experts warn, following the release of a global trust survey.

items.title: Popular song lyrics express less emotion over time, analysis of 38K+ songs finds
items.snippet: New research from Michigan State University finds that popular music has gradually become less explicit about emotion and relationships—both across generations of artists and within artists' careers.

items.title: During El Niño, a perfect storm of weather systems could spell disaster for the Great Barrier Reef
items.snippet: The strong El Niño currently under way in the Pacific Ocean raises the specter of marine heat waves and coral bleaching once again threatening Australia's iconic Great Barrier Reef. And now new research has revealed the complex interplay of atmospheric patterns and weather systems thousands of kilometers apart that can combine in a recipe potentially fatal for coral reefs.

items.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
items.snippet: Research suggests listening more while talking less. Killing aimless meetings can help, too.
